what_its_for: Riluzole is used to treat ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), also called Lou Gehrig's disease. It does not cure ALS, but it can help slow the disease and may help you live longer by protecting nerve cells in your brain and spinal cord.
how_to_take: Take riluzole by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. Tablets and film strips should be taken on an EMPTY stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal. The oral suspension (liquid form, Tiglutik) should be shaken well before each use and can be taken with or without food. Swallow the oral film strip (Exservan) by placing it on your tongue and letting it dissolve — do not chew or swallow it whole. Always take your doses at the same times each day (usually once in the morning and once in the evening, about 12 hours apart) to keep a steady level of medicine in your body.
dosing: The usual dose for adults is 50 mg taken twice a day, about 12 hours apart (for example, 8 AM and 8 PM). Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how you respond to the medicine and how well your liver is working. Never take more or less than your doctor prescribes.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regularly scheduled time. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are not sure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store tablets and oral film strips at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Store the oral liquid (Tiglutik) upright in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze the liquid. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking riluzole, as it can increase the risk of liver damage. Avoid eating high-fat meals right before taking your dose, especially for tablets and film strips, as food can reduce how well the medicine is absorbed. Be careful with activities that require alertness, like driving or operating machinery, until you know how this medicine affects you, as it may cause dizziness or drowsiness. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, because some medications (including certain antibiotics, antidepressants, and heartburn medicines) can interact with riluzole and affect how it works or increase side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice), dark or tea-colored urine, severe stomach pain, nausea or vomiting that won't stop, unusual tiredness or weakness, fever, shortness of breath or new cough, or a significant decrease in urination. Also call your doctor if you notice any new or unusual symptoms. Your doctor will order regular blood tests (especially liver function tests) to check that the medicine is not causing harm — do not skip these appointments.
when_it_works: Riluzole works continuously in the background to help protect your nerve cells. You may not feel or notice an obvious improvement in your symptoms. This medicine helps slow the progression of ALS rather than reversing damage that has already occurred. It is important to keep taking it every day, even if you do not feel a difference, and to follow up regularly with your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults (65+): Use with caution; your doctor may monitor you more closely for side effects, especially liver problems. Liver disease: Riluzole is broken down by the liver. If you have liver problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or avoid this medicine. Tell your doctor if you have any history of liver disease or drink alcohol regularly. Kidney disease: Use with caution; let your doctor know if you have kidney problems. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking riluzole if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The risks and benefits should be discussed carefully. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been fully established; use only under close medical supervision.
